lower-0862-s8-place-value-rounding.description: Use tenths and hundredths, order negative decimals and round to significant figures.

sections.title: How does dividing by 0.1 change a number?
sections.label: Tenths
sections.intro: Imagine cutting a length into tenths. A whole metre contains ten tenths.

blocks.html: Multiplying by 0.1 divides by 10. Dividing by 0.1 multiplies by 10. Use 100 for hundredths.

figure.alt: One tenth and a whole
figure.caption: Ten pieces of size one tenth make one whole. Count tenths when you divide by 0.1.

blocks.prompt:
A label shows a length of \(4.5\) m.

Calculate \(4.5\) ÷ \(0.01\).
blocks.hint: Make the divisor 1 by scaling both numbers.
blocks.solution:
\(0.01\) is one of 100 equal parts of 1. Dividing counts how many of these parts fit.

Multiply both numbers in the division by 100. The divisor becomes 1.

\(450\)

retry.feedback: The result must grow. Dividing by a number between zero and one counts smaller groups.

blocks.html: A division does not always make a number smaller. Ask how many parts fit.

blocks.prompt:

blocks.hint: Make the divisor 1 by scaling both numbers.
blocks.solution:

Multiply both numbers in the division by 10. The divisor becomes 1.

\(46\)

retry.feedback: The result must grow. Dividing by a number between zero and one counts smaller groups.

blocks.html: Use an inverse calculation to check the result.

sections.title: Where do significant figures start?
sections.label: Rounding
sections.intro: Significant figures tell us how much detail to keep.

blocks.html: Start at the first non-zero digit. Keep the required number of digits. Use the next digit to round and leave zeroes where they hold place value.

sections.title: Which negative number is smaller?
sections.label: Order
sections.intro: Write both decimals to the same number of places.

blocks.html: Compare the position on the number line. Moving left makes the value smaller even when its distance from zero grows.

figure.alt: Two negative values on a number line

Write the lower reading.

Farther left means smaller. For negative readings, the greater distance from zero gives the smaller reading.

lower-0862-s8-integer-calculations.description: Apply the calculation order and explain sign rules for integers and powers.

sections.title: What happens to the sign?
sections.label: Signed
sections.intro: Use gains and losses to picture the operation.

blocks.html: Estimate with nearby friendly numbers to check the size. Then multiply or divide the magnitudes. Matching signs give a positive result. Different signs give a negative result.

figure.alt: Two negative values on a number line
figure.caption: Negative five is to the left of negative three, so it is smaller.

blocks.prompt:
Each move lowers a marker by 8 points. A game counts 4 moves.

Calculate the overall change.
blocks.hint: Multiply the magnitudes and apply the sign.
blocks.solution:
Each move is \(-8\). The magnitude of the change is \(8\times 4=32\). One negative factor gives a negative result.

\(-32\)

retry.feedback: Falling describes a negative change.

blocks.html: Adding negatives has a different sign rule from multiplying negatives.

blocks.html: Use the inverse operation to check the sign of a quotient.

sections.title: What must I calculate first?
sections.label: Order
sections.intro: Work from the structure of the expression, rather than simply left to right.

blocks.html: Evaluate brackets first, then powers and roots. Multiply and divide, then add and subtract. Read equal-priority operations left to right.

blocks.prompt:
An activity card shows \(16+2\times(3^2-3)\).

Calculate its value.
blocks.hint: Work through brackets, powers, multiplication and addition.
blocks.solution:
Inside the bracket, calculate \(3^2=9\) first. The bracket becomes \(6\).

Next multiply \(6\) by 2. Then add 16.

\(28\)

retry.feedback: Finish the multiplication before adding the first number.

blocks.html: Addition does not come before multiplication unless brackets say so.

sections.title: When can I combine powers?
sections.label: Indices
sections.intro: An index tells you how many times to use a base as a factor.

blocks.html: For a common non-zero base, add exponents to multiply and subtract to divide. Dividing a power by itself gives a zero exponent and value 1.

blocks.prompt:
An expression contains \(3^4\times 3^4\) and \(3^4\div 3^4\).

Write the product as a power of 3. Give the power.
blocks.hint: Add exponents on powers that share a base.
blocks.solution:
The first power contains 4 copies of 3 multiplied together. The second contains 4.

The product therefore has \(4+4=8\) copies.

\(8\)

retry.feedback: Count all the copies of the base. Add the exponents.

blocks.html: Do not add the exponents when adding the powers.

blocks.hint: Add exponents on powers that share a base.

\(8\)

retry.feedback: Count all the copies of the base. Add the exponents.

blocks.html: Keep the base unchanged when giving the combined power.

sections.title: Can a root be negative?
sections.label: Roots
sections.intro: A square repeats a factor twice. A cube repeats it three times.

blocks.html: The square of a negative number is positive. The square root symbol gives the non-negative root of a non-negative number. A negative number can have a negative cube root.

blocks.prompt:

Find \(\sqrt[3]{-216}\).
blocks.hint: Find the signed number whose cube is the negative card.
blocks.solution:

\(-6\)

retry.feedback: The cube of a positive number is positive.

lower-0862-s8-factors-multiples.description: Use common factors and multiples and classify whole and rational numbers.

sections.title: Which group size divides both totals?
sections.label: Factors
sections.intro: If every item must be used, each total must divide exactly by the number of groups.

blocks.html: A factor divides a number exactly. To find the highest common factor, compare factor lists or use the common prime factors.

figure.alt: Factor tree for 36
figure.caption: The branches give 36 as 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. Different trees give the same prime factors.

blocks.prompt:
A class has 36 wooden counters and 40 card squares. All objects must be used.

What is the greatest number of identical packs they can make?
blocks.hint: Find the highest common factor of the two counts.
blocks.solution:
A possible pack count divides both 36 and 40 exactly.

The common factors are 1, 2, 4. The greatest is \(4\).

\(4\)

blocks.html: The highest common factor cannot be more than the smaller total.

blocks.prompt:
A class has 42 wooden counters and 40 card squares. All objects must be used.

What is the greatest number of identical packs they can make?
blocks.hint: Find the highest common factor of the two counts.
blocks.solution:
A possible pack count divides both 42 and 40 exactly.

The common factors are 1, 2. The greatest is \(2\).

\(2\)

blocks.html: Check both divisions leave no remainder.

sections.title: When will two patterns meet again?
sections.label: Multiples
sections.intro: A repeated interval generates a list of multiples.

blocks.html: The lowest common multiple is the first positive number that is a multiple of both inputs.

blocks.prompt:
A workshop has bells that ring every 16 minutes and every 5 minutes. They ring together at opening.

How many minutes later will they ring together again?
blocks.hint: Find the lowest common multiple.
blocks.solution:
Write multiples of 16 and 5. The first positive number on both lists is 80.

\(80\) minutes

blocks.html: The product is a common multiple but a smaller one may exist.

blocks.prompt:
A workshop has bells that ring every 17 minutes and every 5 minutes. They ring together at opening.

How many minutes later will they ring together again?
blocks.hint: Find the lowest common multiple.
blocks.solution:
Write multiples of 17 and 5. The first positive number on both lists is 85.

\(85\) minutes

blocks.html: In a repeating event question, do not count the first meeting as the next one.

sections.title: Where does a number belong?
sections.label: Families
sections.intro: A number may belong to more than one family.

blocks.html: The natural numbers are counting numbers. The integers include positive whole numbers, negative whole numbers and zero. A rational number can be written as a fraction of integers with non-zero denominator.

blocks.prompt:
One tile shows \(-\frac{36}{5}\). Another tile shows \(-7\).

Which is the smallest family containing \(-\frac{36}{5}\)?
blocks.hint: Check whether the fraction is an integer.
blocks.solution:
\(-\frac{36}{5}\) is a ratio of integers with a non-zero denominator. The division has a remainder, so the value is not an integer.

Rational numbers

blocks.html: A written fraction can simplify to an integer. Check the value before classifying.

blocks.prompt:
One tile shows \(-\frac{41}{5}\). Another tile shows \(-8\).

Which is the smallest family containing \(-\frac{41}{5}\)?
blocks.hint: Check whether the fraction is an integer.
blocks.solution:
\(-\frac{41}{5}\) is a ratio of integers with a non-zero denominator. The division has a remainder, so the value is not an integer.

Rational numbers

blocks.html: Use the smallest family that contains the number when asked.

examples.title: Making identical activity packs
examples.question:
A class has 30 wooden counters and 30 card squares. All objects must be used.

  1. What is the greatest number of identical packs they can make?

    [2]

  2. How many objects are in each pack?

    [2]
solution: (a) A possible pack count divides both 30 and 30 exactly.
The common factors are 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30. The greatest is \(30\).

sections.title: Which terms can I collect?
sections.label: Meaning
sections.intro: A letter can name a changing quantity in an expression. A formula links quantities. An equation asks where two expressions are equal.

blocks.html: Terms are like terms only if they have the same variable part, including the powers. Combine their coefficients and keep the variable part.

blocks.prompt:
A learner writes \(8x+3x^2-2x\).

Collect the terms and simplify.
blocks.hint: Combine only like terms.
blocks.solution:
The terms \(8x\) and \(-2x\) use the same power of x. Combine their coefficients.

The squared term has a different power and stays separate.

blocks.html: x and x² are different terms.

sections.title: What changes in this situation?

blocks.html: A one-off charge is not multiplied by the number of items.

sections.title: How do I remove brackets?

sections.intro: An area model splits a product across both parts of a bracket.

blocks.html: Multiply the outside factor by each inside term. Multiply coefficients and add exponents for matching bases.

blocks.prompt:

Expand the brackets.
blocks.hint: Multiply every term by the outside factor.

The second product keeps the minus sign.

sections.title: How do I put brackets back?
sections.label: Factorise
sections.intro: Take out the factor shared by every term.

blocks.html: Find the highest common factor of the coefficients and the lowest power of each shared letter. Divide every term by this factor to find what remains in the bracket.

blocks.prompt:

What is the highest common factor of both terms?
blocks.hint: Find the numerical factor and the lowest shared power.
blocks.solution:
The integers 63 and 72 have highest common factor 9 because 7 and 8 are consecutive.

Both terms contain x, while only the first includes a second x factor.

\(9x\)

lower-0862-s8-equations-intervals.description: Use inverse operations to solve equations, rearrange formulae and interpret interval boundaries.

sections.title: How do I balance an equation?
sections.label: Balance
sections.intro: An equation says both sides have the same value. Imagine a balanced scale: taking the same amount from both pans keeps it balanced. We can use that idea to leave the unknown on one side.

blocks.html: Simplify each side first. Then add or subtract the same term on both sides so that the variable terms collect together. Undo the remaining operations, and substitute your answer into the original equation.

blocks.prompt:
Plan P costs \(13x+25\) credits. Plan Q costs \(16x+4\) credits. The number of uses is x.

Find the number of uses for which the plans cost the same.
blocks.hint: Equate the two costs and subtract \(13x\) from both sides. What still needs to be balanced?
blocks.solution:
Set the expressions equal. Subtract \(13x\) from both sides to leave \(25=3x+4\).

Subtract 4 from both sides and divide by 3.

\(7\)

retry.feedback: Keep the same operations on both sides. Check the number of uses in both plans.

blocks.html: When removing \(2x\) from one side, subtract \(2x\) from both sides. Changing only one side breaks the equality.

blocks.prompt:
Plan P costs \(2x+32\) credits. Plan Q costs \(6x+4\) credits. The number of uses is x.

Find the number of uses for which the plans cost the same.
blocks.hint: Subtract \(2x\) from both sides, then subtract \(4\) from both sides.
blocks.solution:
Set the expressions equal. Subtract \(2x\) from both sides to leave \(32=4x+4\).

Subtract 4 from both sides and divide by 4.

\(7\)

retry.feedback: Keep the same operations on both sides. Check the number of uses in both plans.

blocks.html: If \(x\) counts a number of uses, check that the solution makes sense as a whole number of uses.

sections.title: What if an equation contains a fraction?
sections.label: Fraction
sections.intro: A fraction bar divides everything written above it. In \(\frac{t+4}{3}\), add \(4\) to \(t\) first, and then divide by \(3\). To undo the expression, use the inverse steps from the outside in.

blocks.html: Multiplying both sides by the denominator removes a fraction. If a side has more than one term, multiply every term on that side. For \(\frac{x}{5}-2=3\), adding \(2\) first keeps the numbers simpler.

blocks.prompt:
A mystery number t is shared into 5 equal amounts. After giving away 2, one share has 3 left.

Find t.
blocks.hint: Write \(\frac{t}{5}-2=3\). Undo the subtraction of \(2\) before the division by \(5\).
blocks.solution:
The equation is \(\frac{t}{5}-2=3\). Add 2 to both sides.

Multiply both sides by 5 to find the original amount.

\(25\)

retry.feedback: Add the amount back to the share before multiplying by the number of shares.

blocks.html: \(\frac{x+6}{3}\) means \(\frac{x}{3}+2\), not \(\frac{x}{3}+6\). The denominator applies to the whole numerator.

blocks.prompt:
A mystery number t is shared into 5 equal amounts. After giving away 2, one share has 4 left.

Find t.
blocks.hint: The share was \(2\) larger before anything was given away. Put the five original shares together.
blocks.solution:
The equation is \(\frac{t}{5}-2=4\). Add 2 to both sides.

Multiply both sides by 5 to find the original amount.

\(30\)

retry.feedback: Add the amount back to the share before multiplying by the number of shares.

blocks.hint: Multiply both sides by \(5\), using brackets around \(x-2\).

retry.feedback: The \(5\) multiplies both terms on the right, giving \(5x-10\).

blocks.html: After your final line, check the numerator and division separately in the original equation.

sections.title: How can I make another letter the subject?
sections.label: Subject
sections.intro: A formula describes a link between quantities. The subject is the letter on its own. Change the subject when you want the formula to give another quantity directly, such as finding width from area and length.

blocks.html: Treat the other letters as fixed quantities while you undo the operations on the desired subject. For \(P=5t-7\), add \(7\) to both sides first, then divide by \(5\): \(t=\frac{P+7}{5}\). You can keep an answer in letters and use it for different inputs.

blocks.prompt:
A score is given by \(P=11t-8\), with t the number of sessions.

The score is 14. Find the session count.
blocks.hint: Use \(14=11t-8\). Add \(8\) before dividing by \(11\).
blocks.solution:
Use \(14=11t-8\). Add 8, then divide by 11.

\(2\)

blocks.html: \(\frac{P+7}{5}\) divides the whole sum by \(5\). Writing \(\frac{P}{5}+7\) changes the formula.

blocks.prompt:
A score is given by \(P=12t-8\), with t the number of sessions.

The score is 16. Find the session count.
blocks.hint: With the score set to \(16\), add \(8\) to recover the value of \(12t\).
blocks.solution:
Use \(16=12t-8\). Add 8, then divide by 12.

\(2\)

blocks.html: Put a known value back into the original formula once you have rearranged it. It should give the same result as the new formula.

sections.title: Does the boundary count?
sections.label: Interval
sections.intro: An inequality describes a set of permitted values. A strict sign such as \(\lt\) leaves out the boundary. A sign such as \(\le\) includes it. Check whether the question restricts the values to whole numbers.

blocks.html: Read \(2\lt x\le5\) as “greater than \(2\) and at most \(5\)”. On a number line, use an open dot at \(2\) and a filled dot at \(5\). Both conditions must be true at once.

figure.alt: Number line with an open and a filled endpoint
figure.caption: The open circle excludes 2. The filled circle includes 5. The interval is greater than 2 and at most 5.

blocks.prompt:

Write the largest allowed age.
blocks.hint: Look at the \(\le\) beside \(18\). Is \(a=18\) permitted?
blocks.solution:
The right-hand end is \(18\).

The sign includes equality, so the end value is allowed.

\(18\)

retry.feedback: The upper endpoint is allowed because the sign includes equality.

blocks.html: The value \(2\) makes \(2\lt x\) false, despite being at the edge of the line segment. A nearby value such as \(2.1\) can work if decimals are allowed.

blocks.prompt:

blocks.solution:

\(19\)

retry.feedback: The upper endpoint is allowed because the sign includes equality.

blocks.prompt: How many integers \(n\) satisfy \(-3\lt n\le2\)?
blocks.hint: Start with the first integer after \(-3\). Include \(2\) if it meets both conditions.
blocks.solution: \(-2,-1,0,1,2\) satisfy the inequality, so there are \(5\).

retry.feedback: \(-3\) is excluded by the strict lower inequality. Begin your list at \(-2\).

blocks.html: Test each endpoint in the original statement separately. Words such as “at least” and “at most” include equality.

examples.title: Find when costs are equal
examples.question: One club charges \(3x+2\) credits and another charges \(2x+7\) credits for \(x\) sessions. For how many sessions are the costs equal?
solution: Set the costs equal: \(3x+2=2x+7\). Subtract \(2x\) from both sides to get \(x+2=7\).
Subtract \(2\) from both sides: \(x=5\).
At five sessions the plans cost \(3(5)+2=17\) and \(2(5)+7=17\) credits.

examples.title: Find a length from a perimeter
examples.question: A rectangle has sides of length \(x+2\) cm and \(2x-1\) cm. Its perimeter is \(38\) cm. Find both side lengths.
solution: The sum of one long and one short side is \(38\div2=19\). Write \(x+2+2x-1=19\).
Collect terms: \(3x+1=19\). Subtract \(1\) and divide by \(3\) to find \(x=6\).
The lengths are \(8\) cm and \(11\) cm. Their doubled sum is \(38\) cm.

examples.title: Reverse a division and a subtraction
examples.question: A rope of length \(L\) metres is cut into five equal pieces. After \(2\) metres are removed from one piece, it is \(4\) metres long. Find \(L\).
solution: Write \(\frac{L}{5}-2=4\). Add \(2\) to both sides to get \(\frac{L}{5}=6\).
Multiply both sides by \(5\): \(L=30\).
Each piece is \(6\) metres before the cut, so it becomes \(4\) metres after losing \(2\).

examples.title: Remove a denominator on both sides
examples.question: Solve \(\frac{x+4}{3}=x-2\).
solution: Multiply both sides by \(3\): \(x+4=3(x-2)=3x-6\).
Add \(6\) and subtract \(x\) on both sides. This gives \(10=2x\), so \(x=5\).

examples.title: Find the time for one stage
examples.question: The total time in minutes is \(T=3s+5\), where \(s\) is the time in minutes for one of three identical stages. Make \(s\) the subject and use it when \(T=26\).
solution: Subtract the five-minute wait: \(T-5=3s\).
When \(T=26\), this gives \(s=\frac{21}{3}=7\) minutes.

examples.title: Find the width from a formula with brackets
examples.question: The perimeter of a rectangle is \(P=2(l+w)\). Make \(w\) the subject.
solution: The outside operation is multiplication by \(2\). Divide both sides by \(2\): \(\frac{P}{2}=l+w\).
Subtract \(l\) from both sides: \(w=\frac{P}{2}-l\).
Check with \(l=7\) and \(P=20\). The new formula gives \(w=3\), and \(2(7+3)=20\).

examples.title: Read open and closed ends
examples.question: Let \(n\) be an integer with boundaries \(-2\) and \(4\). The lower boundary is included and the upper boundary is excluded. Write the inequality and list the possible integers.
solution: Write \(-2\le n\lt4\). The endpoint \(-2\) can be used because equality is allowed there.
The possible integers are \(-2,-1,0,1,2,3\). The next integer, \(4\), makes the upper comparison false.

examples.title: Combine two restrictions
examples.question: A parcel with mass \(m\) kg must have \(m\lt7\). To qualify for a different label, it must also have \(3.5\le m\). Can a parcel of mass \(3.5\) kg or \(7\) kg use that label? Give the combined inequality.
solution: Combine the restrictions in order: \(3.5\le m\lt7\). The mass must satisfy both statements.

revision.body:
Keep both sides balanced

\(3x+2=2x+7\) gives \(x+2=7\), then \(x=5\). Check both original sides.

Undo the outside operation

\(\frac{x+4}{3}=x-2\) gives \(x+4=3(x-2)\). Apply the multiplication to each term.

Isolate the subject

\(P=2(l+w)\) gives \(w=\frac{P}{2}-l\).

Check both boundaries

sections.title: How can a decimal be exact and keep going?

sections.intro: A bar above a digit or group of digits means it repeats indefinitely.

The result is \(9x=32\) where x is the original number. Divide both sides by 9.

blocks.hint: This is six tenths multiplied by seven hundredths. What unit does one tenth of one hundredth give?

retry.feedback: Seven hundredths is \(0.07\). Count one place from \(0.6\) and two from \(0.07\).

blocks.html: Use a bound: \(0.06<0.1\), so \(0.7\times0.06<0.07\). An answer above that bound signals a place-value error.

sections.title: What can I do with a decimal divisor?
sections.label: Quotient
sections.intro: Division can ask how many small amounts fit into a total. For example, pouring water into cups of \(0.4\) litres might give several cups per litre.

blocks.html: Scale the dividend and divisor by the same power of ten until the divisor is a whole number. For example, \(2.8\div0.04=280\div4\). Each quantity is now expressed in hundredths, so the number of groups stays the same.

figure.alt: Seven tenths in three pairs of two tenths, with one tenth left over
figure.caption: With \(0.7\) litres and \(0.2\)-litre cups, there are three full cups and \(0.1\) litres left. Counting tenths gives \(7\div2\).

blocks.prompt:
A tube contains \(9.8\) litres of water. Each full test container takes \(0.7\) litres.

How many full containers can be filled?
blocks.hint: Measure both amounts in tenths of a litre: how many groups of \(7\) tenths are in \(98\) tenths?
blocks.solution:
Scale both amounts by 10. Dividing \(9.8\) by \(0.7\) becomes \(98\) divided by 7.

Scaling numerator and divisor by the same factor preserves the quotient.

\(14\)

blocks.html: If you change just the divisor, you change the size of each group while leaving the total fixed. The result will count the wrong groups.

blocks.prompt:
A tube contains \(11.2\) litres of water. Each full test container takes \(0.8\) litres.

How many full containers can be filled?
blocks.hint: Write \(11.2\) litres and \(0.8\) litres as counts of tenths before dividing.
blocks.solution:
Scale both amounts by 10. Dividing \(11.2\) by \(0.8\) becomes \(112\) divided by 8.

Scaling numerator and divisor by the same factor preserves the quotient.

\(14\)

blocks.html: For a question about full containers, use the whole-number part of the quotient. Multiply back to see how much remains.

sections.title: Can I make the numbers easier first?
sections.label: Regroup
sections.intro: Look for pairs that make a whole number, or for a small change from a friendly value. A few small mental steps can replace a long calculation.

blocks.html: Grouping terms in a sum can make an easy calculation first. A factor outside brackets also multiplies each term inside: \(a(b+c)=ab+ac\). Choose whichever route gives easier numbers.

blocks.prompt:
A tablet shows \(0.04\times(6.6+(-2.6))\).

Calculate the value efficiently.
blocks.hint: \(6.6+(-2.6)\) means moving back \(2.6\) from \(6.6\). Do that before multiplying.
blocks.solution:
First combine the two values in brackets. They make 4. Next multiply \(0.04\) by 4.

\(0.16\)

blocks.html: In \(a(b-c)\), the factor applies to both \(b\) and \(c\). Applying it to only the first term changes the value.

blocks.prompt:
A tablet shows \(0.04\times(6.7+(-2.7))\).

Calculate the value efficiently.
blocks.hint: Compare the two numbers inside the brackets: what is \(6.7-2.7\)?
blocks.solution:
First combine the two values in brackets. They make 4. Next multiply \(0.04\) by 4.

\(0.16\)

blocks.html: Keep the sign with its number when regrouping. In \(7.6+(-2.6)+1.4\), the pair \(7.6-2.6\) gives \(5\).

sections.title: Which amount is 100%?
sections.label: Percentage
sections.intro: The amount before a change is \(100\%\). A \(15\%\) rise adds \(15\%\) of that amount. A \(15\%\) fall leaves \(85\%\) of it. The same percentage can mean different amounts in different situations.

blocks.html: Use a multiplier to find the new amount in one step: \(1.15\) after a rise of \(15\%\) and \(0.85\) after a fall of \(15\%\). To find the percentage change from two given values, divide the change by the original amount, then multiply by \(100\%\).

figure.alt: The original amount and a twenty per cent addition
figure.caption: The whole is the original amount. A 20% increase adds two tenths of that whole.

blocks.prompt:
A screen price of 20 credits increases by 15%.

Work out the new price.
blocks.hint: Find \(10\%\) and \(5\%\) of \(20\). Add both to the starting price.
blocks.solution:
The change is 15% of 20, which is \(3\) credits.

Add the change. The new price is \(23\) credits.

\(23\) credits

retry.feedback: That is the size of the change. Apply it to the original price.

blocks.html: A reduction from \(80\) to \(60\) is \(25\%\) because the original amount is \(80\). Dividing by \(60\) uses the value after the change.

blocks.prompt:
A screen price of 25 credits increases by 15%.

Work out the new price.
blocks.hint: Use \(1.15\) as the multiplier for a rise. The total must be greater than \(25\).
blocks.solution:
The change is 15% of 25, which is \(\frac{15}{4}\) credits.

Add the change. The new price is \(\frac{115}{4}\) credits.

\(\frac{115}{4}\) credits

retry.feedback: That is the size of the change. Apply it to the original price.

blocks.prompt: A bike hire price falls from \(50\) to \(40\) credits. Give the percentage decrease.
blocks.hint: The starting price stands for \(100\%\). Compare the drop of \(10\) with that starting price.
blocks.solution: The decrease is \(\frac{50-40}{50}\times100\%=20\%\).

retry.feedback: \(25\%\) compares the drop with the new price. Divide the change by the original \(50\) credits.

blocks.html: Write the original amount beside \(100\%\) before choosing a multiplier or dividing to find a percentage.

examples.title: Place the point by using the estimate
examples.question: A board is \(2.4\) m long and \(0.15\) m wide. Work out its area.
solution: The width is between \(0.1\) m and \(0.2\) m, so the area is between \(0.24\) and \(0.48\) square metres.
Multiply \(24\times15=360\). The original factors were \(10\) times and \(100\) times smaller.
Divide \(360\) by \(1000\) to get \(0.36\) square metres. It fits the estimate.

examples.title: Decide which slab has the larger area
examples.question: Slab A is \(0.8\) m by \(0.65\) m. Slab B is \(1.2\) m by \(0.45\) m. Which has the larger area, and by how much?
solution: The longer side alone cannot decide this: slab B is longer but narrower.
The areas are \(0.8\times0.65=0.52\) and \(1.2\times0.45=0.54\) square metres.
Slab B is larger by \(0.54-0.52=0.02\) square metres.

examples.title: Count full cups and find the leftover
examples.question: There are \(3.5\) litres of juice. A full cup holds \(0.4\) litres. Find the number of full cups and the juice left.
solution: Count in tenths of a litre: \(3.5\div0.4=35\div4=8.75\).
There is enough for \(8\) full cups, using \(8\times0.4=3.2\) litres. A ninth cup would need \(3.6\) litres in total.
The amount left is \(3.5-3.2=0.3\) litres.

examples.title: Choose the smallest number of pieces
examples.question: A workshop needs a cable at least \(2.6\) metres long. Short pieces of length \(0.35\) metres can be joined end to end without any loss. How many pieces are needed?
solution: Find \(2.6\div0.35=260\div35\). This is between \(7\) and \(8\) because \(7\times35=245\) and \(8\times35=280\).
Seven pieces give \(2.45\) metres, too short. Eight pieces give \(2.8\) metres, which meets the requirement.
Choose \(8\) pieces. Here the length is a minimum to reach, so the number of pieces goes up to the next integer.

examples.title: Make a whole inside the brackets
examples.question: Calculate \(0.35(8.4-3.4)\) without a calculator.
solution: The bracket is \(8.4-3.4=5\). Use it before multiplying.
\(0.35\times5\) is half of \(0.35\times10\), so the result is \(1.75\).

examples.title: Use a nearby friendly value
examples.question: Work out \(12\times0.49\) mentally and explain your method.
solution: \(0.49\) is \(0.5-0.01\). The two products \(12\times0.5\) and \(12\times0.01\) are quick to find.
Calculate \(12(0.5-0.01)=6-0.12=5.88\). It is just below \(6\), as expected.

examples.title: Calculate the sale price
examples.question: A coat costing \(64\) credits is reduced by \(25\%\). Find the new price.
solution: A \(25\%\) reduction leaves \(75\%\), or three quarters, of the original price.
One quarter of \(64\) is \(16\). Three quarters is \(3\times16=48\) credits.
Check by subtracting the discount: \(64-16=48\) credits.

examples.title: Compare two percentage changes
examples.question: A model kit falls in price from \(40\) to \(34\) credits. A book falls from \(30\) to \(24\) credits. Which has the larger percentage reduction?
solution: Both prices fall by \(6\) credits. Each reduction is measured against its own original price.
The kit reduction is \(\frac{6}{40}\times100\%=15\%\). The book reduction is \(\frac{6}{30}\times100\%=20\%\).
The book has the larger percentage reduction because the same change makes up more of its starting price.

lower-0862-s8-ratio-proportion.description: Compare like units, share among several parts and find a constant unit rate.

sections.title: What needs to match before I write a ratio?
sections.label: Units
sections.intro: A ratio compares quantities in a stated order. In a length ratio, “red to blue” means red comes first. The ratio should be the same whether both lengths are measured in metres or both in centimetres.

blocks.html: Use a common unit first, then divide each term by the same number. In \(18:24\), dividing both terms by \(6\) gives \(3:4\). The ratio has no units once both measurements use the same unit.

blocks.prompt:
A red cord is \(\frac{27}{10}\) m long. A blue cord is 50 cm long.

Give the ratio red : blue in its simplest whole-number form.
blocks.hint: Convert \(\frac{27}{10}\) m into \(270\) cm. Then simplify \(270:50\).
blocks.solution:
Convert the red cord to 270 cm so both lengths use centimetres. Then cancel the common factors of 270 and 50.

First cancel 10 and then reduce the remaining ratio.

\(27:5\)

blocks.html: Writing \(1.2:80\) for \(1.2\) m and \(80\) cm compares different units. Convert the first number to \(120\) cm before simplifying.

blocks.prompt:
A red cord is \(\frac{14}{5}\) m long. A blue cord is 50 cm long.

Give the ratio red : blue in its simplest whole-number form.
blocks.hint: Use centimetres for both cords. The first term will be greater because the red cord is longer.
blocks.solution:
Convert the red cord to 280 cm so both lengths use centimetres. Then cancel the common factors of 280 and 50.

First cancel 10 and then reduce the remaining ratio.

\(28:5\)

blocks.html: Read the final ratio aloud in the order asked. If one quantity is larger, its term should be larger too.

sections.title: How much is one part of a share?
sections.label: Sharing
sections.intro: The values in a sharing ratio count equal-sized parts. If a ratio is \(2:3:4\), the whole uses nine equal parts, but the first share gets just two of them.

blocks.html: Decide what amount you know. If you know the total, divide by the sum of the terms. If you know one share, divide by the term for that share. Then scale up from one part.

figure.alt: Three groups shown as equal-sized parts in a strip
figure.caption: There are nine equal parts in total. Share the total among these parts before grouping them.

blocks.prompt:
Three teams share 52 tokens in the ratio \(3:8:2\).

Find the first team’s share.
blocks.hint: There are \(3+8+2\) equal parts. The first share is three of those parts.
blocks.solution:
The ratio has 13 parts. Divide 52 by 13 to find 4 tokens for one part.

The first team has 3 of these parts.

\(12\)

blocks.html: Dividing a total by the largest ratio term only works when that number counts all the parts. Add the ratio terms to count the whole.

blocks.prompt:
Three teams share 56 tokens in the ratio \(4:8:2\).

Find the first team’s share.
blocks.hint: Find one part from \(56\div(4+8+2)\) and then count four copies of it.
blocks.solution:
The ratio has 14 parts. Divide 56 by 14 to find 4 tokens for one part.

The first team has 4 of these parts.

\(16\)

blocks.prompt: Ava and Bo share cards in the ratio \(2:7\). Bo gets \(21\) cards. How many cards are there altogether?
blocks.hint: Match the given \(21\) to Bo’s \(7\) parts. Once you have one part, count all the parts.
blocks.solution: Each part contains \(21\div7=3\) cards. There are \(2+7=9\) parts, so there are \(27\) cards.

retry.feedback: \(6\) is Ava’s share. Add Bo’s \(21\) cards to get the total.

blocks.html: When you find every share, add them to recover the total. When one share is given, check against that share instead.

sections.title: When is a relationship directly proportional?
sections.label: Proportion
sections.intro: Two quantities are directly proportional when scaling one by a factor scales the other by the same factor. One pen costing \(3\) credits means two cost \(6\), three cost \(9\), and zero cost zero if there is no extra charge.

blocks.html: Check whether the value per unit stays constant: divide the total by the quantity for each row. A fixed fee on top of a unit price changes the cost per item, so the total with that fee is not directly proportional to the quantity.

blocks.prompt:
The total cost of 7 identical notebooks is 70 credits. Each one costs the same and there is no starting fee.

Find the cost of 15 notebooks.
blocks.hint: Divide \(70\) by \(7\) to find one notebook’s cost, then multiply by \(15\).
blocks.solution:
Divide 70 by 7 for the cost of one notebook, 10 credits. Then multiply by 15.

\(150\) credits

blocks.html: A constant addition to the total for each extra item does not automatically make the two quantities directly proportional. Check for a starting charge.

blocks.prompt:
The total cost of 8 identical notebooks is 80 credits. Each one costs the same and there is no starting fee.

Find the cost of 17 notebooks.
blocks.hint: At \(80\) credits for eight, find the price of one before using \(17\) notebooks.
blocks.solution:
Divide 80 by 8 for the cost of one notebook, 10 credits. Then multiply by 17.

\(170\) credits

blocks.prompt: \(4\) litres of paint cover \(28\) square metres. With the same coverage per litre, how many litres are needed for \(63\) square metres?
blocks.hint: First find the area covered by one litre. Then count how many of those areas fit in \(63\).
blocks.solution: Each litre covers \(28\div4=7\) square metres, so \(63\div7=9\) litres are needed.

retry.feedback: \(7\) is square metres per litre. Divide the total area by \(7\) to find litres.

blocks.html: Use the unit rate if there is no easy scale factor. Keep its units in your working, such as credits per notebook.

examples.title: Compare ribbon lengths in different units
examples.question: A yellow ribbon is \(1.2\) m long. A green ribbon is \(80\) cm long. Give yellow : green in simplest form.
solution: Convert the yellow length: \(1.2\) m is \(120\) cm.
Yellow : green is \(120:80\). Divide each term by \(40\) to get \(3:2\).
Yellow is longer, so its ratio term \(3\) is greater than \(2\).

examples.title: Decide which mix has more concentrate
examples.question: Mix A uses \(120\) mL concentrate and \(360\) mL water. Mix B uses \(150\) mL concentrate and \(600\) mL water. Which has the higher proportion of concentrate?
solution: Simplify concentrate : water. Mix A is \(1:3\) and mix B is \(1:4\).
Both have one part concentrate. That is one quarter of mix A and one fifth of mix B.
Mix A has the higher proportion of concentrate. The larger amount of concentrate in mix B came with more water.

examples.title: Share a total among three clubs
examples.question: Three clubs share \(54\) badges in the ratio \(2:3:4\). Find the number for each club.
solution: There are \(2+3+4=9\) parts, so one part is \(54\div9=6\) badges.
The shares are \(2\times6=12\), \(3\times6=18\) and \(4\times6=24\).

examples.title: Start with one known share
examples.question: Dan and Sam share stickers in the ratio \(3:5\). Sam gets \(30\) stickers. How many stickers are there altogether?
solution: The \(30\) stickers belong to Sam, so they correspond to \(5\) parts. Each part contains \(30\div5=6\) stickers.
The whole has \(3+5=8\) parts, giving \(8\times6=48\) stickers.

examples.title: Scale a recipe up
examples.question: Four people need \(300\) g of rice. Using the same amount per person, find how much rice is needed for six people.
solution: Find the amount for one person: \(300\div4=75\) grams.
Six people need \(6\times75=450\) grams.
You can also multiply both quantities by \(\frac{6}{4}=\frac32\).

examples.title: Test both hire plans for direct proportion
examples.question:
The table gives two hire plans. Which total cost is directly proportional to the number of hours?

Costs in credits

solution: For plan A the costs per hour are \(4\div1=4\), \(8\div2=4\) and \(12\div3=4\).
For plan B, the one-hour cost is \(7\), but the two-hour cost is \(11\div2=5.5\) per hour.
Plan A is the proportional plan. Plan B’s table fits a fixed fee of \(3\) credits plus \(4\) per hour.

Find the first team’s share.
extraPractice.hint: Find the value of one of the \(2+3+3\) parts. The first team gets two.
extraPractice.solution:
The ratio has 8 parts. Divide 32 by 8 to find 4 tokens for one part.

The first team has 2 of these parts.

\(8\)

Three teams share 36 tokens in the ratio \(3:3:3\).

Find the first team’s share.
extraPractice.hint: All three ratio terms are equal, so the teams each get one third of the total.
extraPractice.solution:
The ratio has 9 parts. Divide 36 by 9 to find 4 tokens for one part.

The first team has 3 of these parts.

\(12\)

extraPractice.prompt:
The total cost of 9 identical notebooks is 108 credits. Each one costs the same and there is no starting fee.

Find the cost of 19 notebooks.
extraPractice.hint: Use \(108\div9\) to find the shared price per notebook.
extraPractice.solution:
Divide 108 by 9 for the cost of one notebook, 12 credits. Then multiply by 19.

\(228\) credits

extraPractice.prompt:
The total cost of 10 identical notebooks is 120 credits. Each one costs the same and there is no starting fee.

Find the cost of 21 notebooks.
extraPractice.hint: Find the cost of one notebook from \(120\div10\), then scale it to \(21\) notebooks.
extraPractice.solution:
Divide 120 by 10 for the cost of one notebook, 12 credits. Then multiply by 21.

\(252\) credits

lower-0862-s8-probability-models.description: Use complements and sample spaces and compare observed and predicted chances.

sections.title: What remains when an event does not happen?
sections.label: Complement
sections.intro: The complement of an event includes all outcomes in which that event does not happen. If “green” is the event and a spinner has three colours, “not green” includes both of the other colours.

blocks.html: An event and its complement never happen together and cover every outcome. Their probabilities add to \(1\), so \(P(\text{not }A)=1-P(A)\).

blocks.prompt:
Each segment on a spinner is equally likely. The spinner has 30 segments, with 1 painted green and the others painted purple.

What is the probability of not landing on green?
blocks.hint: There are \(30\) equally likely segments. How many are outside the event “green”?
blocks.solution:
The probability of green is \(\frac{1}{30}\). Green and not green include every result, so their probabilities add to 1.

Subtract \(\frac{1}{30}\) from 1.

\(\frac{29}{30}\)

retry.feedback: That is the probability of green. Find the probability of the other outcome.

blocks.html: If the question asks for “not blue”, include every other outcome, even if several colours are possible.

blocks.prompt:
Each segment on a spinner is equally likely. The spinner has 31 segments, with 1 painted green and the others painted purple.

What is the probability of not landing on green?
blocks.hint: Keep the total of \(31\) in the denominator. Subtract one green segment from the total to get the numerator.
blocks.solution:
The probability of green is \(\frac{1}{31}\). Green and not green include every result, so their probabilities add to 1.

Subtract \(\frac{1}{31}\) from 1.

\(\frac{30}{31}\)

retry.feedback: That is the probability of green. Find the probability of the other outcome.

blocks.html: Before subtracting from \(1\), say in words what each of the two events includes.

sections.title: How can I list every pair once?
sections.label: Sample space
sections.intro: In a two-step experiment, use an ordered pair to record the two results. Keep the first result in the first position, even if the second result is smaller.

blocks.html:
Use one row for each possible first result and one column for each possible second result. The total number of pairs is the number of rows times the number of columns. If both devices are fair and independent, each of these pairs is equally likely.

solution: Use row \(3\) for spinner A and column \(2\) for spinner B. The entry is \((3,2)\).

examples.title: Compare two totals

examples.title: Use a complement for a range of sums
examples.question: Two independent fair spinners each show \(1,2,3\) or \(4\). Find the probability that their total is at least \(4\).
solution: There are \(16\) possible pairs. Counting the outcomes below \(4\) is shorter: \((1,1)\), \((1,2)\) and \((2,1)\).
Subtract the probability of those three outcomes from \(1\): \(1-\frac3{16}=\frac{13}{16}\).

examples.title: Compare two trial sets using relative frequency
examples.question: A fair spinner should land on blue half the time. Trial A gives \(11\) blues in \(20\) spins. Trial B gives \(64\) blues in \(100\) spins. Which observed proportion is nearer to one half?
solution: The two observed proportions are \(\frac{11}{20}=0.55\) and \(\frac{64}{100}=0.64\).
The gaps from \(0.5\) are \(0.05\) and \(0.14\), so trial A is closer.
A had fewer trials. An individual larger sample is not guaranteed to be closer.

examples.title: Combine two sets with different sizes

solution: Add successes to get \(8+33=41\). Add trial counts to get \(20+60=80\).
The combined relative frequency is \(\frac{41}{80}=0.5125\).
Averaging \(0.4\) and \(0.55\) would give the two runs the same weight, although the second has three times as many spins.

Enlarge a figure by scale factor 2 with centre \((-2,-2)\). Its vertex P is \((-1,0)\).

  1. Find the image coordinates of P.

    [2]

  2. A side is 7 cm long on the original. Find its new length and say what happens to its angles.

    [2]
solution: (a) Start at the centre and move 1 across and 2 up to reach P. Make both movements 2 times as large.
Add the new displacement to the centre.
(b) Lengths multiply by the scale factor. The shape keeps its angles.
14 cm. Angle sizes are unchanged.

examples.title: Identify the integer scale of an enlargement
examples.question:
An enlargement of centre \((-1,2)\) takes P \((7,6)\) to P′ \((15,10)\).

  1. Find the scale factor.

    [2]

    [2]
solution: (a) The old horizontal displacement from the centre is 8. The new horizontal displacement is 16.
The vertical displacements scale from 4 to 8, confirming the same factor.
(b) Repeat for another pair of matching points to locate the centre if it is unknown.
The original point, its image and the centre should lie on the same line.

revision.body:
What must I know to turn a point?

Think about the displacement from the centre. For a 90° clockwise turn, right becomes down and up becomes right. For 90° anticlockwise, right becomes up and up becomes left. A 180° turn reverses both moves.

From where do I measure an enlargement?

Draw a ray from the centre through a vertex. Multiply the distance from the centre by the same positive scale factor along each ray. A point at the centre stays fixed.

How can the image tell me the scale?

For a pair away from the centre, compare image distance with original distance. If the centre is unknown, draw two non-parallel lines joining two pairs and use their crossing.

sections.title: Should I record a category, a count or a measurement?
sections.label: Types
sections.intro: Start with the question you want your data to answer.

blocks.html: Categorical data give a label. Discrete numerical data can only take separate values, such as counts. Continuous data are measurements that can take any value in an interval.

blocks.prompt:
A survey team invites 28 learners and records each learner’s chosen route colour.

What type of data will this variable give?
blocks.hint: Decide whether the value is a category, a count or a measurement.
blocks.solution:
Colours are categories, even when a spreadsheet replaces each colour name with a code.

Categorical

sections.title: Who should be in my sample?
sections.label: Sample
sections.intro: The population is the group you want to describe. The sample is the part you actually study.

blocks.html: A convenience sample is quick but may miss some groups. Random selection helps avoid preference. A systematic sample takes every kth item after a start and can miss patterns if the list is periodic.

figure.alt: Four steps for a sampling investigation
figure.caption: Plan the question and sampling before collecting data. Revise the plan after a small trial if necessary.

blocks.prompt:
A school wants to estimate lunch choices across 22 classes. A team first asks only the 3 learners in a sports club.

Which method would give better coverage of the whole school?

options.A: Select a sample at random from each class, allowing for class sizes
options.B: Ask the same club a second time
options.C: Ask only the people nearest the door

blocks.hint: Match the sample to the population of interest.
blocks.solution:
Include every class in the sampling plan, then draw names without preference within each class.

Select a sample at random from each class, allowing for class sizes

blocks.html: A bigger sample can still be biased if all members come from one group.

sections.title: How can a short trial improve a survey?
sections.label: Trial
sections.intro: Try the question with a few people before using it with the full sample.

blocks.html: Check that the question is clear, is fair and gives the type of data you need. Change unclear instructions or units, then try again.

revision.body:
Where do I put people who belong to both groups?

In a Venn diagram, the middle overlap shows both properties. In a Carroll diagram, each cell shows one yes-or-no combination. Tally marks can record counts as data arrive.

How do I use row and column totals?

Add across rows for one property and down columns for the other. An unknown cell is often a total with the known entries removed.

When should I put bars together or stack them?

Dual bars make same-category comparisons easy. Compound bars show category totals as stacks, with each component coloured or patterned and labelled in a key.

How does a count become an angle?

A sector is the same fraction of 360° as the category is of the total count. Divide frequency by the total, then multiply by 360°.
